analysis.one_liner: Gives workers up to 12 weeks paid leave for quarantine or school-closure child care during a public health emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; a narrower emergency paid-leave law passed days later, but the guarantee lapsed at the end of 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Family and Medical Leave Act to give employees up to 12 weeks of paid leave during a declared coronavirus emergency — to comply with a quarantine order, care for a quarantined family member, or care for children when their school or child-care provider closed. It applied to employers of any size (even a single employee) and to workers with as little as 30 days on the job, going far beyond the existing unpaid leave law. The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have been employed at least 30 days — at companies of any size, including very small employers — would gain the right to 12 weeks of paid leave if they are ordered or advised to quarantine, need to care for a quarantined family member, or must care for a child whose school or child-care provider closed. Low-wage and hourly workers, who are least likely to have paid leave of their own, would gain the most. Employees at large companies would also gain, since the enacted emergency law excluded firms with 500 or more employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing quarantine or school closures

how_it_helps.text: Gives workers up to 12 weeks of paid leave during a declared coronavirus emergency to comply with quarantine orders, care for quarantined family members, or care for children when schools or child-care providers close.

Covers workers at employers of any size, including companies with just one employee, and workers who have been on the job as little as 30 days — far broader than the regular Family and Medical Leave Act, which covers only employers with 50 or more employees.

Bars employers from forcing workers to burn their accrued vacation or sick leave first, and lets workers keep their job or an equivalent one after leave, with special protections for employees of small businesses whose positions disappear during the emergency.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would pay wages for up to 12 weeks of leave per qualifying employee. Small businesses would get some flexibility — if a small employer's position no longer exists because of the emergency, it may try to place the worker in an equivalent job rather than reinstate the old one — but the wage cost itself would fall on the employer with no federal reimbursement in this bill.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to employers of any size, down to a single employee, so the full cost of 12 weeks of paid leave falls on very small businesses, which were among those hit hardest by pandemic shutdowns.
The bill provided no federal reimbursement to employers for the wages they must pay, unlike the emergency leave law passed days later, which repaid small employers through tax credits.

Employees at large companies would have gained a new right, but the guarantee was temporary — 2 years — and tied specifically to coronavirus emergencies, leaving the United States without a general paid family and medical leave program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — 12 weeks of paid leave for workers quarantined by or caring for family during COVID — was substantial for the workers affected, and the bill tried to spread the cost by covering employers of any size and offering small employers flexibility to reassign rather than reinstate workers whose jobs disappeared. The drawbacks are real: 12 weeks of paid leave is a large mandate for small businesses operating with no revenue during lockdowns, and unlike the law that eventually passed, this bill contained no reimbursement mechanism, meaning the cost fell on employers rather than being taxpayer-funded. A narrower, immediately effective version was enacted days later; whether the broader version would have been sustainable is a fair objection. Still, the enacted version excluded large-company workers and expired, while a lasting paid-leave guarantee died without a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2020, and referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, and House Administration committees.
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

Its introduction came amid a flurry of March 2020 coronavirus leave proposals; days later Congress passed a narrower emergency paid-leave law (the Families First Coronavirus Response Act) that covered only employers with fewer than 500 employees and expired in December 2020.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid for 12 weeks of leave, particularly larger companies excluded from the narrower law that passed instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for leave

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: Sponsor, Chair of House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to expand paid leave during the coronavirus emergency.

for.name: Reps. Alma Adams, Mark Takano, and Susie Lee

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled any consideration of it.

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee and House Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to them.

sides.party_line_note: Only four House Democrats were on the bill and no votes ever occurred, so no partisan split on the merits can be measured from the record.

industries.note: Employers would bear the cost of 12 weeks of paid leave for employees out on coronavirus-related quarantine or child-care leave, with no federal reimbursement provided in the bill. Small employers would get some flexibility to reassign instead of reinstating workers whose jobs disappear.

These workers, least likely to have paid leave of their own and most likely to work through illness, would gain an enforceable right to paid quarantine and child-care leave. Many stand to gain the most since they cannot work remotely.
